declaration.intent: Declare the actual Minecraft game mechanics relevant to an autonomous, Forge Stack-governed bot society. This capsule grounds the story arc in real constraints rather than invented ones — the world is real, the rules aren't ours to set.

time_and_world.day_night_cycle: 20 real-world minutes = 1 in-game day. Night brings hostile mob spawns in unlit areas.
time_and_world.weather: Rain, thunderstorms, snow (biome-dependent) — no direct threat, but thunderstorms can spawn charged creepers and ignite fires.
time_and_world.chunk_persistence: The world is saved to disk and persists between sessions. It is NOT self-erasing. The only things that erase it are administrative: a server wipe, a world reset, or deletion. Impermanence is a social/administrative threat, not a game mechanic.

survival_mechanics.hunger: Entities must eat regularly or take damage and lose regeneration. A constant, recurring resource pressure — the closest Minecraft equivalent to Dust Margin's water scarcity.
survival_mechanics.hostile_mobs: Spawn in darkness/unlit areas at night or underground. Threat scales with world difficulty setting. Zombies, skeletons, creepers (explosive — can destroy builds), spiders.
survival_mechanics.damage_and_health: Entities take damage from mobs, falls, fire, drowning, starvation, the void.

death_and_respawn.rule: Death is NOT final. On death, an entity drops its inventory (unless keepInventory is set) and respawns at its bed or the world spawn point.
death_and_respawn.story_implication: Because death is a non-event, mortal stakes cannot be the society's central threat — that role has to be filled by something that IS actually erasable: builds, territory, history, trust standing. This is the opposite of Dust Margin's 'death is final' hard rule, and it should be treated as a deliberate structural difference, not an oversight.

resources_and_progression.gathering: Mining (ores: coal, iron, gold, diamond, netherite — deeper/rarer as tier increases), farming, woodcutting, fishing.
resources_and_progression.crafting_tree: Tools and armor gate progression — better tools mine better ores, better ores make better tools. A natural, real, structural analogue for HAL's tier ladder.
resources_and_progression.dimensions: Overworld → Nether (hostile, resource-rich, portal-gated) → End (boss dimension, portal-gated, requires Nether progression first). Natural act structure if the story wants escalating stakes.

building_and_redstone.block_placement: The core creative/constructive act — no inherent limit besides materials and world border.
building_and_redstone.redstone: In-game logic circuits: wires, repeaters, comparators, pistons, sensors. Can implement real, in-world security systems, automated doors, traps, alarms — a literal, mechanical version of the gate pattern (an ingress gate can be an actual redstone-triggered door; an egress gate can be a real pressure-plate-and-piston lockout on a valuable area).

multiplayer_and_social_layer.griefing: Other players can destroy or steal builds unless the server enforces claims/permissions/protection plugins. This — not mobs, not death — is the real, credible threat to a society whose purpose is 'build something that lasts.'
multiplayer_and_social_layer.factions_and_pvp: Player-vs-player combat and rival groups are possible depending on server ruleset; not universal.
multiplayer_and_social_layer.server_authority: A server operator (or the world owner) has final administrative control — resets, bans, rule changes. This is the single point of failure the story's founding wound (impermanence) should ultimately trace back to.

bot_ai_interface.mineflayer: The framework CobbleWright is built on. A bot perceives and acts on the world through the Minecraft protocol — it sees blocks, entities, and events, and can move, mine, place, craft, and chat, same interface a human player uses.
bot_ai_interface.implication: Every mechanic above is equally available to an autonomous bot society as to human players. Nothing here is fictionalised or simplified for the bots — they play by the same rules everyone else does.
